‘Rings of Power’ returns with a struggle for air superiority

Warning: Light Spoilers for the latest season ahead.

By Shannon Corbeil

Published Nov 17, 2026 7:33 PM PST

0

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” is back with season three, dropping the first four episodes on Nov. 11, 2026 (very likely as a thank you for our service)—and with them, a little peek at some aerial combat.

Very minor spoilers ahead for LOTR: ROP Season Three, Episode Four , “Gundabad.”

Also Read: Russia’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ is the story from Mordor’s point of view

Galadriel enlists the aid of Landroval, the Great Eagle, who finds himself in peril—giving me very stressful “Game of Thrones” Viserion flashbacks. But for everyone who asks why Frodo didn’t just ride a Great Eagle to Mordor, well, orcs have had anti-air artillery since at least the Second Age of Middle Earth, thousands of years before the fellowship leaves Rivendell.

And that’s not all. Sauron has the Fell Beast.

Let’s get nerdy.

The Great Eagles

The Great Eagles, sometimes simply referred to as “the Eagles,” are enormous, sentient eagle-like creatures in Tolkien’s Middle Earth lore. In “The Hobbit,” we’ve seen them rescue Thorin’s company from goblins and Wargs and join the Battle of the Five Armies. In “The Lord of the Rings,” they come to Gandalf’s aid again to rescue him from Orthanc after Saruman’s treachery. They also join in at the Battle of Morannon, helping to fight against Sauron’s own air force of Nazgûl who mount flying beasts known as “hell hawks” or “fell beasts.”

And of course, the Great Eagles arrive in time to rescue Frodo and Sam from the eruption of Mount Doom. 

But the creatures have a much longer history in Middle Earth, one that goes back to the First Age when they served as messengers for Manwë, the King of the Valar and brother of the Dark Lord Melkor (Morgoth, whom Sauron refers to often in “The Rings of Power” and who was the one to plunge Middle Earth into darkness during the First Age). 

The Valar were divine, immortal spirits who served as guides for Elves and Men on Middle Earth. They served as emissaries for Ilúvatar, the omniscient and omnipotent creator of the world.

During the First Age, the Eagles fought alongside the army of the Valar during the War of Wrath and helped to destroy the majority of the dragon population. 

In “The Rings of Power,” which takes place during the Second Age, we have seen the Great Eagles before; one arrived in Season Two Episode Three, “The Eagle and the Sceptre” during the coronation of Queen Míriel in Númenor, allowing Pharazôn to claim the Eagle arrived to support his political bid instead (also…thanks, Eagle, for not clearing that up for some reason?). In “The Rings of Power” this event will lead to the downfall of Númenor. 

And now here we are, in season three, with Landroval getting all shot at and making my heart drop. Kill all the humans you want, television and filmmakers, but don’t hurt animals! I can’t take it! 

The Fell-Beast

In Tolkien history, fell-beasts fought in the First Age on the side of Morgoth—even against the Great Eagles. In “The Rings of Power,” Sauron explains that the creatures were once Eagles themselves until Morgoth “blessed them with his touch and taught him to crave his lash.”

There isn’t a lot of consistency in Tolkien’s canon regarding fell-beasts. In “The Return of the King,” he gave the following description:

“The great shadow descended like a falling cloud. And behold! it was a winged creature: if bird, then greater than all other birds, and it was naked, and neither quill nor feather did it bear, and its vast pinions were as webs of hide between horned fingers; and it stank. A creature of an older world maybe it was, whose kind, lingering in forgotten mountains cold beneath the Moon, outstayed their day, and in hideous eyrie bred this last untimely brood, apt to evil. And the Dark Lord took it, and nursed it with fell meats, until it grew beyond the measure of all other things that fly; and he gave it to his servant to be his steed.”

(Note, Tolkien does not name the creature here and even uses the word “fell” to describe the meats the creature ate; Tolkien often used “fell” as a signifier of evil or decay.)

So it’s a bit of a creative choice on the part of the “Rings of Power” creators to introduce a creature known so far just as “The Beast” and declare that they were corrupted by Morgoth, similarly to how he corrupted Elves to create Orcs.

And while the orcs may have trouble controlling The Beast, you will find that Sauron does not.

Air Superiority

We are mid-way through Season Three, with episodes five and six to be released on Nov. 18 and episodes seven and eight on Nov. 25 and here’s where we stand:

The Great Eagles appear to have taken a clear stand in Galadriel’s fight against Sauron. 

Sauron’s forces have AAA that can take down an Eagle—but now Galadriel knows this. 

What she doesn’t know, however, is that now Sauron has an air force of his own.

Hey, at least it’s not dragons, right? (While Morgoth bred and commanded dragons in the First Age, Sauron never quite mastered the skill.)
